tier_reason: First-party maintainer (fanatid) comment of 2021-03-18 in PR #53 gives WASM vs tiny-secp256k1@1.1.6 elliptic numbers on i5-8250U and Apple M1; bench code is public (benches/index.js) but Node version, Rust/wasm-opt flags and benchmark repetitions are not stated, so not A, and nothing independent, so not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: PR #53 maintainer comment, Intel i5-8250U Linux: sign WASM 469.03 us/op (2132.07 op/s) vs tiny-secp256k1@1.1.6 elliptic 913.58 us/op (1094.60 op/s); verify WASM 605.01 us/op vs elliptic 2576.87 us/op; pointFromScalar WASM 280.10 us/op vs elliptic 542.96 us/op. Apple M1: sign WASM 133.19 us/op vs elliptic 522.64 us/op; verify WASM 212.05 us/op vs elliptic 1515.26 us/op; pointFromScalar WASM 96.43 us/op vs elliptic 316.96 us/op. Author summary: 'Wasm vs js: 2x for sign and pk creation, 4x for verify'. The Rust N-API addon in the same PR did sign in 51.71 us/op on the i5-8250U, about 9x faster than WASM (derived from page data). README (no numbers): the wasm2js asm.js build is 10x-20x slower than WASM and noble-based @bitcoinerlab/secp256k1 is 1.5x-5x slower than WASM.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust >= 1.50.0, wasm32-unknown-unknown target, wasm-opt from binaryen (README build section); the PR mentions -Z build-std=panic_abort,std and opt-level variants for the addon, but no wasm-opt flags or Node.js version are given for the benchmark run
corrections.caveats: Numbers are a 2021 maintainer comment in PR #53, which was closed unmerged ('Moved to #55'), so they were measured on pre-release code; the Rust N-API addon that beat WASM by about 9x was not shipped (it is commented out of the current benches/index.js and the README describes the current version as WASM only), and the old 1.1.6 C++ NAN addon is also faster than WASM per the README ('faster than elliptic but slower than node bindings'). Against the category's other baseline, the same library compiled natively, WASM loses. Node.js version, wasm-opt flags and repetition counts are not stated; no independent measurement. libsecp256k1 (bitcoin-core/secp256k1) is already catalogued; this entry is its WASM packaging.

notes: Numbers in the record match the PR comment exactly; added the pointFromScalar rows and the comment anchor the README links to. Main shortcomings: first-party 2021 numbers from an unmerged PR, no Node or flag details, and the WASM build is about 9x slower than a native addon of the same library.

tier_reason: README table (wasmoon 15.267 ms vs fengari 389.923 ms) is first-party; the harness (bench/comparisons.js, bench/heapsort.lua) and the release build flags (build.sh: emcc -O3) are public, but no CPU model, Node.js or fengari version is stated, so not A.

corrections.workload: Heap sort (bench/heapsort.lua): one timed call that sorts 2,000 random numbers ten times and asserts the order, including parsing the Lua source; harness bench/comparisons.js times a single cold run of each VM with console.time (fengari first, then wasmoon) in one Node process.
corrections.claimed_speedup: README: wasmoon 15.267 ms vs fengari 389.923 ms for the whole ten-iteration heap sort call (about 25.5x, derived from page data); README text says wasmoon runs Lua much faster than Fengari unless there is a lot of JS to Lua interop.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: emcc -O3 with emmalloc, WASM_BIGINT, ALLOW_MEMORY_GROWTH (build.sh release path); the README does not say which build produced the table, and its local build instructions use the -O0 dev build
corrections.caveats: One single-shot micro-benchmark (no repetitions or warm-up) with no CPU model, Node.js, browser or fengari version and no date. The timed region covers all ten sorts plus parsing, so it is the total of the ten runs, not per run. The README warns that heavy JS-Lua interop can erase the advantage, and fengari is smaller (214 kB vs 393 kB plain). First-party. Lua itself (lua/lua) is already catalogued, and no comparison against native Lua (the category's same-library-native baseline) is given.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; the bench code resolves the 'per run or ten runs' ambiguity (ten runs in one timed call). Main shortcomings: single cold run, no hardware or runtime versions, first-party only, no native-Lua comparison.
